Aggregate

/AG-rih-git/ - the stress falls on AG · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Aggregate means a total formed by combining separate parts.

Investors watch the fund's aggregate, not the fate of any single stock inside it.

Worked Example

The city's recycling report prints one number in bold: the aggregate collected from its six depots. Taken alone, the smallest depot looks like a failure — half-empty trucks, a yard that never fills. Folded in with its five larger siblings, though, that modest stream helps push the citywide result past ten thousand tons, and the program keeps its funding for another year.

Aggregate is the exact word for that bold number, because aggregate means a total formed by combining separate parts — six depots, one whole. An average would divide everything back down to a typical depot; a sum you might take of anything, but aggregate insists on the gathering: scattered pieces deliberately brought together.

How Aggregate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

total

total: the everyday word for the whole; aggregate stresses that separate parts were combined to get there

sum

sum: arithmetic's word for numbers added; an aggregate can gather anything countable

Antonyms

fraction

fraction: one part of the whole, never the whole

component

component: a single piece considered on its own

How Strong Is It? — sample → subtotal → aggregate

sample vs. aggregate

sample vs. aggregate: A sample counts only a handful of the parts — it hints at the whole without adding anything up.

subtotal vs. aggregate

subtotal vs. aggregate: A subtotal stops short of the aggregate — one section summed, with the rest still waiting to be counted.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of aggregate.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ag-

Prefix — ag-: to, toward (Latin ad-, assimilated)

Root — greg

Root — greg: flock, herd (Latin grex)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: forming nouns and verbs

Put it together

Put it together: Ag- (toward) + greg (flock) + -ate = herded together into one flock. Latin grex was a herd of animals; an aggregate is a whole built by driving scattered items into a single total, and the flock is still faintly visible whenever forty lists become one figure.

Use the root in a new word: segregate

Use the root in a new word: segregate: Se- means apart, so to segregate the noisy campers is to move them apart from the flock — the same greg, pointed the other way.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / technical

Aggregate is the accountant's and planner's word — reach for it when the point is that a whole was built from separate parts. In this unit it faces the other direction from allocate: aggregating pulls shares together into one total, allocating deals a total out into shares. For everyday talk, total or sum does the job.
